title: The Umbrella That Wasn't Mine
scene: It starts raining while you are having lunch at a café. You notice a plain black umbrella by the door, briefly convince yourself it might be yours, then discover from one small detail — and one silent look — that it definitely is not.
sceneJa: カフェで昼食中に雨が降り始める。入口にある黒い傘を一瞬自分のものだと思い込み持ち出すが、木製の持ち手で違うと気づく。返しに戻ると、本当の持ち主らしい男性と無言で目が合う。

questions.question: Which boundary is most natural?
options: whether I had brought one after all / and simply forgotten about it
whether I had / brought one after / all and simply / forgotten about it
whether / I had brought one / after all and simply forgotten / about it
questions.explanation: The first chunk contains the reconsidered possibility — maybe the speaker did bring an umbrella after all — and the second adds the possible explanation for not remembering it.

questions.question: What does ‘after all’ mean in ‘whether I had brought one after all’?
options: The speaker is reconsidering an earlier belief and wondering if the opposite might be true
The speaker is saying the umbrella was the last object in the café
The speaker has finally decided to buy an umbrella
questions.explanation: Here, ‘after all’ signals a change or reconsideration: the speaker had believed they brought no umbrella, but briefly wonders whether they actually did.

questions.question: Why is ‘Neither of us said anything’ awkward rather than reassuring?
options: Because the silence strongly suggests that both people understand what has just happened
Because neither person can speak English
Because the man has not noticed the umbrella
questions.explanation: The silence communicates more than a direct accusation would: the man appears to recognise the umbrella, and the speaker knows that he knows.

speak: Start calmly, with mild resignation about the rain. Give ‘whether I had brought one after all’ a slightly hopeful lift. At ‘I had never owned an umbrella like that,’ let the certainty arrive quietly rather than dramatically. Pause after ‘looked at the umbrella,’ then again after ‘then looked at me.’ Keep the final sentence completely matter-of-fact; the humour comes from treating embarrassment as useful information.
review: Flow: rain problem → convenient possibility → self-persuasion → small physical clue → immediate retreat → silent social confirmation → dry reframing. Useful chunks are ‘after all,’ ‘I had never owned ... like that,’ and ‘Neither of us ...’. Unlike recent lessons where the speaker rationalises continuing, this one turns on a quick correction followed by an awkwardly precise social moment.
